say.text: A 40-year-old labourer at a district hospital in rural India has small bowel obstruction. He has had no abdominal surgery.
A PYQ asks for the most common cause here. Which is the keyed answer?

choices.label: Adhesive bands, the usual adult cause

say.text: Yes. PYQs expected an obstructed or strangulated hernia in India and developing countries.
The setting words and the 'no surgery' line point there. Hernia comes first in the adult virgin abdomen.
Tempting: adhesions are the commonest cause of adult small bowel obstruction, so they feel like the answer everywhere.
But this stem names India and no surgery. The PYQ key expected the hernia there, so the setting decides which answer is keyed.
Hold both: PYQs said hernia in India; current practice in a surgical setting says adhesions.

sure_note.text: You were sure of adhesions. Adhesions are the usual Western answer, so reread the setting words before you name a cause.

say.text: Tempting: adhesive bands are the usual adult cause, so any adult with obstruction feels like an adhesion case.
Adhesions need a previous operation. This patient has none, so the adhesion model does not fit his history.
In a virgin abdomen check the hernial orifices first. Hernia comes before tumour.

sure_note.text: You were sure of bands with no surgery in the history. Read the history line before you name an adult cause.

say.text: Adhesive obstruction, day 2. The pain was colicky and is now constant. Pulse 118, with guarding over one area of the abdomen.
What is the best next step?

choices.label: Continue conservative care, this is colic

say.text: Yes. Constant pain, tachycardia and localised guarding suggest strangulation or peritonitis.
Fluids, potassium, an NG tube and antibiotics come first, then theatre, because the strangulation signs override any wait.
Tempting: the 72-hour trial is the rule you learnt for adhesive obstruction, so waiting feels like the safe default.
But the trial only follows once strangulation, peritonitis, a hernia and a closed loop are excluded. Here constant pain and guarding exclude it.
What is right: resuscitate, then theatre. The trial is for simple adhesive obstruction without strangulation.

sure_note.text: You were sure the trial applied. Screen for strangulation before any time limit.

say.text: Tempting: colic is the classic picture of simple obstruction, so a change in the pain is easy to miss.
The key word is constant. Persistent severe pain with tachycardia and localised guarding points to strangulation.
What is right: resuscitate, then theatre, because the wait ends when the loop is compromised.

sure_note.text: You were sure of simple colic. A change from colicky to constant pain is the cue to look again.

say.text: Tempting: the operation feels decisive, and the patient is unwell, so the theatre seems the fastest fix.
But vomiting and sequestration cause dehydration and electrolyte loss. Operating on that patient first adds risk.
What is right: drip and suck, then laparotomy. Resuscitation is the first step even when the bowel is dying.
You just named strangulation. Now the reason, which is what the exam tests.
Why does constant pain with tachycardia mean the loop is strangulated?

choices.label: Venous return is blocked, so the loop becomes ischaemic
The colic has grown stronger, so the bowel works harder
Absent sounds mean a paralysed bowel, so this is ileus

say.text: Yes. Rising intraluminal pressure first blocks venous return, then arterial inflow, so the wall becomes ischaemic.
Acidosis and toxic products follow, which is why a raised lactate and constant pain mean surgery, not waiting.
Tempting: pain is the classic colic of obstruction, so a stronger colic seems the natural explanation.
But colic comes from peristaltic waves against a block. Constant pain comes from a loop whose blood supply is failing.
What is right: venous block and ischaemia explain the constant pain and the tachycardia together.
Tempting: silent bowel is the bedside clue most people remember, so it feels like paralysis is the cause of the pain.
But absent sounds fit paralytic ileus and late peritonitis. They do not explain constant pain in a strangulated loop.
What is right: venous block and ischaemia, which is why the pain is constant.
Adhesive obstruction on a Gastrografin study. The contrast reached the colon within 24 hours.
What does that predict?

choices.label: Operate at 48 hours, the second look
Operate at 72 hours, the trial's limit

say.text: Yes. Contrast in the colon within 24 hours predicts that the obstruction will resolve without surgery.
The 24-48 hour window is the second look for doubtful bowel, and 72 hours is the limit of the trial.
Tempting: 24-48 hours is the second-look window in surgery, so it feels like the decision point.
But the second look is for bowel that looks doubtful at operation. It does not decide a contrast result.
What is right: a 24-hour contrast result predicts resolution, and 72 hours is the limit.
Tempting: 72 hours is the number everyone quotes, so it feels like the moment to decide.
But 72 hours is the limit for failure of the trial. A 24-hour contrast result already tells you the trial is working.
What is right: contrast in the colon by 24 hours predicts resolution without surgery.
An adult with obstruction has a tender, irreducible swelling in the femoral region. He passes flatus, has no vomiting, and his lactate is rising.
What is the mechanism?

choices.label: Part of the wall is trapped, not the whole lumen
A complete closed loop is trapped in the sac
A Meckel's diverticulum is the sac's content

say.text: Yes. Richter's hernia traps only part of the bowel circumference, so it can strangulate without complete obstruction.
Vomiting and distension can be absent. The warning is pain, tenderness and a rising lactate.
Tempting: strangulated hernia is taught as a complete closed loop with early vomiting, so that picture comes first.
But a closed loop obstructs both ends. Richter's involves only part of the wall, and passing flatus fits partial trapping.
What is right: part of the wall is trapped, and the lumen may stay partly open.

sure_note.text: You were sure of a complete loop. Richter's is the hernia that strangulates without obstructing, so keep the two apart.

say.text: Tempting: Littre's hernia contains a Meckel's diverticulum, and the two eponyms are easy to blur.
But this is partial wall trapping, which is Richter's. Littre's is the hernia that holds the diverticulum.
What is right: part of the wall trapped, the Richter's picture.
Among groin hernias in adults, which one is most likely to strangulate?
Yes. The femoral hernia has the narrowest, most rigid neck of the groin hernias, so it strangulates most readily.
Tempting: the indirect inguinal hernia is the commonest groin hernia, so it feels like the most dangerous one too.
But frequency is not risk. Commonest and most likely to strangulate are two different questions.
What is right: the femoral hernia, because its narrow, rigid neck strangulates most.
Tempting: direct hernias bulge through the medial wall near the femoral region, so they feel like the risky type.
But the risk comes from a narrow, rigid neck, and the femoral hernia has the narrowest one.
What is right: the femoral hernia.
Two stable patients, neither with peritonitis, both with intussusception on ultrasound: a 9-month-old and a 60-year-old.
Which plan fits each patient?

choices.label: Both: air enema reduction under imaging
Both: laparotomy first, before any reduction

say.text: Yes. The child without peritonitis gets image-guided air enema reduction; the adult has a lead point, often a tumour, so it is resected.
Surgery in a child is needed for peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed reduction.
Tempting: enema reduction is the treatment that works in the child, so it feels like the universal cure.
But adult intussusception usually has a lead point, often a tumour. Reducing it by enema can leave the cause behind.
What is right: the child gets an enema, the adult gets resection.

sure_note.text: You were sure the enema cures both. Age is the qualifier. For an adult, ask about a lead point first.

say.text: Tempting: intussusception is an acute abdomen, so theatre feels safest for every patient.
But surgery is needed for peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed reduction. A stable child goes to the enema first.
What is right: a child gets image-guided reduction; an adult with a lead point is resected.
A stable elderly man has sigmoid volvulus on the film. There is no gangrene and no peritonitis.
What is the best management?

choices.label: Endoscopic detorsion and flatus tube, then elective colectomy
Self-expanding stent as the definitive treatment

say.text: Yes. Endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube untwists the bowel, and elective sigmoid colectomy follows because recurrence is common.
Gangrene, perforation or failed detorsion changes this: then emergency resection, usually Hartmann's procedure.
Tempting: a detorsed loop looks healthy on the scope, so stopping there feels complete.
But sigmoid volvulus recurs often after detorsion, so the definitive operation is an elective sigmoid colectomy.
What is right: detorse with a flatus tube, then elective colectomy in the same admission.

sure_note.text: You were sure detorsion ends the care. Recurrence is the reason the colectomy follows.

say.text: Tempting: a stent relieves left-sided malignant obstruction, so it feels like a non-operative cure.
But a stent is a bridge to elective surgery or palliation. This volvulus needs detorsion first, then a planned colectomy.
What is right: detorsion with a flatus tube, then elective sigmoid colectomy.
A plain film of an elderly man shows a massively dilated loop arising from the pelvis, shaped like a coffee bean.
Which diagnosis fits this sign?
Yes. A massively dilated pelvic loop is the coffee bean, or bent inner tube, sign of sigmoid volvulus.
A caecal volvulus gives a different sign: a kidney-shaped caecum displaced to the left upper quadrant.
Tempting: both volvulus types twist the bowel, so one loop shape feels like either of them.
But the caecal sign is a comma or kidney-shaped caecum in the left upper quadrant, not a pelvic coffee bean.
What is right: sigmoid volvulus, the pelvic loop with the coffee bean or bent inner tube sign.
Tempting: intussusception is a common cause of a bowel loop sign, so a familiar loop feels like the answer.
But the intussusception signs are the target and the claw, seen on ultrasound and enema, not a coffee bean on the plain film.
What is right: sigmoid volvulus. Match each sign to its disease and its modality.

sure_note.text: You were sure of intussusception. Each sign belongs to one disease and one modality.

say.text: A stable, fit patient has an obstructing caecal carcinoma.
Which is the operation of choice?

choices.label: Left hemicolectomy, as for most colon cancers
Hartmann's procedure, as for left-sided tumours

say.text: Yes. An obstructing right-sided cancer gets a right or extended right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.
The side of the tumour decides the operation. Left-sided tumours are where Hartmann's or a stent bridge is used.
Tempting: left hemicolectomy is the colon cancer operation most students learn first, so it feels general.
But the side of the tumour decides the operation. A left-sided operation is wrong for a caecal tumour.
What is right: right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.
Tempting: Hartmann's is the usual answer for obstructing colon cancer, so it feels like the safe choice.
But Hartmann's suits left-sided tumours, often unstable. This caecal tumour is right-sided and is resected with anastomosis.
What is right: right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.
An adult has large bowel obstruction with no previous surgery.
Which is the most common cause?
Yes. Colorectal carcinoma is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction in adults.
Volvulus and diverticular disease come next, and the sigmoid is the commonest site of volvulus.
Tempting: volvulus is the classic large bowel picture on a film, so it feels like the most common cause.
But it is a common cause, not the commonest one. In adults, carcinoma leads.
What is right: colorectal carcinoma. Sigmoid is the usual volvulus site.
Tempting: diverticular disease is common in older adults, so its stricture feels like the leading cause.
But diverticular disease comes after carcinoma in adults. Common does not mean most common.
What is right: colorectal carcinoma is the most common cause in adults.
An adult has a large bowel obstruction.
Which cardinal feature comes early?
Yes. In a large bowel block the distal bowel is short and empties first, so absolute constipation comes early.
Distension is marked and vomiting comes late, the reverse of a high small bowel block.
Tempting: profuse vomiting with early distension is the classic picture of obstruction, so it feels like the default.
That is the high small bowel pattern. In a large bowel block vomiting is late and the distension is marked.
What is right: absolute constipation comes early, because the distal bowel empties first.
Tempting: constipation is a late sign in small bowel obstruction, so it feels like a late sign everywhere.
But in a large bowel block constipation is early, and faeculent vomiting is a late sign.
What is right: early absolute constipation, late vomiting.
An adult has suspected small bowel obstruction. The plain X-ray is abnormal.
Which investigation is the definitive test for the cause and for strangulation?

choices.label: Erect and supine abdominal X-ray again

say.text: Yes. Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for small bowel obstruction: it shows the transition point, the cause and strangulation.
The plain film is the first test. It shows the level and which bowel is dilated.
Tempting: the X-ray is the first test and confirms obstruction, so it feels finished.
But the first test answers whether there is obstruction. It does not settle the cause or strangulation.
What is right: contrast-enhanced CT, the definitive test.
Tempting: a barium study shows the bowel directly, so it feels like a definitive study.
But barium must not be given by mouth in suspected large bowel obstruction or perforation, and CT answers the cause and the strangulation.
What is right: contrast-enhanced CT abdomen.
A plain film shows central loops 4 cm across. The caecum measures 7 cm and the transverse colon 5 cm.
Which segment is dilated, and which marker shows it?

choices.label: Small bowel: valvulae conniventes cross the lumen
Caecum: 7 cm, so the caecum is dilated
Large bowel: haustra show on the film

say.text: Yes. Small bowel upper normal is 3 cm, so 4 cm is dilated, and valvulae conniventes that cross the lumen mark small bowel.
The colon limit is 6 cm and the caecum's is 9 cm, so 5 cm and 7 cm are normal.
Tempting: 7 cm looks big for a number you have just met, so the caecum feels distended.
But the caecum's upper normal is 9 cm, so 7 cm is within the limit. The 3-6-9 numbers are not interchangeable.
What is right: the small bowel, 4 cm against an upper limit of 3 cm.
Tempting: haustra are the marker of the colon, so a colon marker on any film feels like the answer.
But haustra do not cross the full width. The folds that cross the lumen mark the small bowel.
What is right: the small bowel, 4 cm, with valvulae conniventes.
Day 3 after abdominal surgery. The abdomen is silent and distended. Potassium is 2.8, and CT shows no mechanical block.
What is the best treatment?

choices.label: Correct potassium, then drip and suck
Laparotomy, since silent bowel means a block

say.text: Yes. Paralytic ileus is treated non-operatively by correcting the cause, especially potassium, with drip and suck.
Silent bowel fits paralysis rather than a mechanical block, so an operation is not the first step.
Tempting: silent bowel is the classic sign of a mechanical block, so it feels like an operation case.
But mechanical block gives high-pitched sounds, and silent sounds fit paralytic ileus. The CT already showed no block.
What is right: correct the potassium, then drip and suck.

sure_note.text: You were sure silence meant a block. In adynamic obstruction the sounds are absent and the cause is treated, not operated.

say.text: Tempting: the 72-hour trial is the rule for adhesive obstruction, so waiting feels cautious.
But this is paralytic ileus with low potassium. The trial is for adhesive obstruction, and the cause must be corrected now.
What is right: potassium correction, drip and suck, and reassessment.
Causes of obstruction are sorted by their relation to the bowel wall.
Which cause lies within the wall?
Yes. A Crohn's stricture narrows the wall itself, so it is intramural.
Adhesive bands sit outside the bowel, which makes them extramural. Faecal impaction sits in the lumen.
Tempting: adhesions cause most obstructions, so a band feels like a cause inside the bowel.
But bands lie outside the bowel and tie it down. They are extramural, not in the wall.
What is right: Crohn's stricture, a narrowing of the wall, is intramural.
Tempting: faecal impaction is a common and dramatic obstruction, so it feels like a wall problem.
But the impacted faeces sit in the lumen. That makes impaction intraluminal, not a wall cause.
What is right: Crohn's stricture is intramural.
Build the take-home. Which one-line summary is best?

choices.label: Level sets the picture; strangulation overrides; resuscitate first
Every obstruction gets a 72-hour trial before a decision
Adhesions are the commonest cause, so start there

say.text: Yes. The level of block gives the picture, strangulation overrides the wait, and resuscitation comes first.
The cards that follow carry these ideas into a new case.
Tempting: the 72-hour rule is the famous number, so it feels like the first rule of the case.
But the trial only follows a screen for strangulation, hernia, closed loop and peritonitis.
What is right: screen first, then resuscitate. The trial is for simple adhesive obstruction.

sure_note.text: You were sure the trial comes first. Screen for strangulation before any time limit.

say.text: Tempting: adhesions are the commonest cause of adult small bowel obstruction, so they feel like the answer everywhere.
But the setting decides. In India PYQs expected hernia, and in a virgin abdomen adhesions are unlikely.
What is right: the level and the setting give the picture, and the cause follows from them.

cards.q: PYQ key versus current practice: most common cause of adult small bowel obstruction in India?
cards.a: PYQs expected an obstructed or strangulated hernia in India and developing countries; adhesions are the most common cause in the West and where surgery is common.

cards.q: Which cardinal feature comes early in a large bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Absolute constipation, because the distal bowel empties first; vomiting is late and distension is marked.

cards.q: Constant severe pain with tachycardia and guarding: what does it mean?
cards.a: Strangulation, from venous block then ischaemia; it needs urgent surgery after resuscitation.

cards.q: Small bowel or large bowel on a plain film: which marker?
cards.a: Valvulae conniventes cross the full width in small bowel; haustra do not cross in large bowel. Upper normal diameters: small bowel 3 cm, colon 6 cm, caecum 9 cm.

cards.q: First test and definitive test for small bowel obstruction in an adult?
cards.a: Plain abdominal X-ray is the first test; contrast-enhanced CT abdomen is the investigation of choice.

cards.q: Coffee bean sign on a plain film?
cards.a: Sigmoid volvulus. Caecal volvulus gives a kidney-shaped caecum in the left upper quadrant.

cards.q: Adhesive obstruction: what does contrast in the colon within 24 hours predict, and when is the trial's limit?
cards.a: Resolution without surgery; the trial's limit is about 72 hours, and strangulation, hernia or closed loop skip the trial.

cards.q: Which groin hernia is most likely to strangulate, and what is Richter's hernia?
cards.a: The femoral hernia, with its narrow rigid neck. Richter's traps part of the wall, so it strangulates without complete obstruction.

cards.q: Intussusception: enema reduction or resection, child versus adult?
cards.a: A child without peritonitis gets image-guided enema reduction; an adult usually has a lead point, often a tumour, and is resected.

cards.q: Sigmoid volvulus without gangrene, and the operation for obstructing right colon cancer?
cards.a: Endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube, then elective sigmoid colectomy; obstructing right-sided cancer gets right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.

cards.q: Paralytic ileus after surgery with low potassium: first treatment? Ogilvie's drug of choice?
cards.a: Correct the potassium and use drip and suck; for Ogilvie's, intravenous neostigmine with cardiac monitoring.
